summaries.Q16640108: Along the ramparts, between the porte de la Ligne and the porte Saint-Joseph, this building stored salt from 1363 so the salt tax could be levied there. Remodelled in 1758 by Jean-Ange Brun, listed in 1984, it was rehabilitated by Jean-Michel Wilmotte in 1989 and now hosts exhibitions and shows, with free entry.
summaries.Q1142988: The city's main museum houses its fine arts in the hôtel de Villeneuve-Martignan, rebuilt from 1741 to designs by Jean-Baptiste Franque and completed in 1749. The town council bought it on 3 March 1833 to make it a museum, around the bequest of Esprit Calvet. The lapidary museum stands separately, rue de la République.
summaries.Q3533155: Built at Villeneuve-lès-Avignon, in the Gard, it stands on the site of an earlier tower put up in 1185 and pulled down by the people of Avignon in 1226. The pariage treaty of 1292 ordered it built near the old port; Randolphe de Mornel finished its first floor in 1303, and a Gothic storey was added around 1360.
summaries.Q22916643: The entrance, rue du Four, is a tall, very plain carriage gateway, on a classical plan between courtyard and garden. Built on a former cardinal's livrée, the house passed to the Galéans family, who added a chapel in 1559; François de Galéans killed Thomas de Baroncelli there on 16 June 1606, after a challenge to a duel.
summaries.Q108699305: Redesigned between 2017 and 2020 from the 2014 excavations, the former papal gardens are part of the palace visitor route. They have three sections: the Pope's garden with its Griffin fountain, at the foot of the Pope's tower, the Palace garden and, below, the Urban V orchard. The planting is Mediterranean.
summaries.Q3462893: At the corner of the rue des Lices and the rue de la République, the building was first the palace begun in 1346 for Queen Joanna I of Naples, who came only once, in 1348. Urban V gave it in 1362 to Cardinal de la Roche. Later a Benedictine priory, then a natural history museum, it was assigned to Reformed worship in 1881.
summaries.Q2957418: On the place du Grand-Paradis, this former 18th-century Catholic chapel is now deconsecrated. Its façades have been listed as historic monuments since 1966, and the building is used as a performance venue during the Festival d'Avignon.
summaries.Q3354545: Decided in 1824 during the laying out of the place de l'Horloge, the theatre stands on the site of the former Benedictine abbey of Saint-Laurent; the first performance was given on 30 October 1825. It burned on 26 January 1846 and was rebuilt on the same site in 1846-1847. After renovation, it reopened in September 2021.
summaries.Q1710718: The oldest lycée in Avignon, rue d'Annanelle, bears the name of its former pupil Frédéric Mistral, Nobel Prize in Literature 1904. Once the royal, then imperial college, it stood near the rue de la République, in the building that became the Petit Lycée. In July, during the Festival d'Avignon, the school is used as a venue.
summaries.Q3329052: Set in the hôtel de Massilian, named after the family that lived there in the 18th century, the museum has shown since 1996 the collection of the Paris couturier and patron Jacques Doucet: Cézanne, Degas, Manet, Van Gogh, Modigliani, Picasso. Two rooms present medieval and Renaissance art gathered by his heirs, the Angladons.
summaries.Q22916655: The dedicatory inscription on the front dates the building to 1619, for Cardinal Scipione Borghese, legate of Pope Paul V; Joseph Girard saw in it the most Italian façade in Avignon. Barracks, then town hall from 1846 to 1852, it took in the music conservatoire in 1860. The city sold it in February 2018 for a boutique hotel.
summaries.Q22916667: Around 1730 Pierre Joseph Jacques de Robert, later lord of Rochegude, bought a house from the La Gratia family, who had brought gilded leather to Avignon, and had it rebuilt in 1732-1733. Its front lines up 9 windows over two storeys and the archivolt keystone bears a faun's head. The gilded room's panelling has been in Paris since 1891.
summaries.Q1200500: Next to the Palais des Papes, this Provençal Romanesque cathedral overlooks the Rhône from the Rocher des Doms. Its porch imitates antique models, with acanthus-leaf capitals. Pius IX gave it the title of minor basilica in 1854; a gilded lead Virgin has crowned the bell tower since 1859, above a carillon of 35 bells.
summaries.Q2957291: On rue Joseph-Vernet, the chapel takes its name from the congregation of the Oratory of Jesus. Begun in 1713, halted, resumed in 1730, it was finished only in 1749: the works wore out several architects. Its plan, two ellipses set within a rectangle, has no equivalent in Avignon. It is the chaplaincy of the lycée Frédéric-Mistral.
summaries.Q15092201: On rue Sainte-Catherine, in the old town, Cistercian nuns settled when Bishop Zoen Tencarari offered them, between 1251 and 1253, refuge inside the city. Their community had been founded as Benedictine in 1060 on the hill of Montdevergues, then took the Cistercian rule around 1150. The church houses the Théâtre du Chêne noir.
summaries.Q2979774: On the place des Carmes, part of the conventual church, it is the only cloister left intact of the mendicant convents that came to Avignon in the 13th century; the Carmelites got the site in 1267. Enlarged under John XXII then Clement VI, long covered by houses, it was cleared in the 20th century. It has hosted the Festival d'Avignon since 1967.
summaries.Q115460879: This early 20th-century building stands at no. 110 rue Joseph-Vernet, south of the town centre. The competition opened in spring 1912 to architects from several departments then planned to build it on the site of the building at 55 rue Théodore-Aubanel. The entries were judged "excellent" and several prizes raised.
summaries.Q3361180: A 15th-century mansion: the Florentine Pierre Baroncelli bought a tavern and neighbouring houses in 1469 for his residence. Frédéric Mistral, who came here in the 19th century, nicknamed it palais du Roure, palace of the oak; it became a home of the Félibrige. Sold in 1908, saved in 1918 by Jeanne de Flandreysy, it holds a regional museum.
summaries.Q22916674: The building contract for this large house was given in 1686 by Charles-Joseph de Joannis, marquis de Verclos, to a mason and a joiner; the design is probably by Louis-François de Royers de La Valfenière. The front, on three planes, faces the place de la Principale. Jean-Baptiste Franque directed works in 1726 and 1748.
summaries.Q22916624: Two houses on the rue de la Croix, at nos. 9 and 11, were joined by an arch after the first was bought in 1685, then sold in 1740 to Joseph de Teste. Armand du Plessis, bishop of Luçon, lodged at no. 9 during his exile, from 1618 to 1619. Bequeathed to the city in 2013, the house is being turned into a contemporary art museum.
summaries.Q1366211: The building stands on the place Jérusalem, on the site the bishop of Avignon set aside in the late 1220s for a new carrière, a quarter closed by three gates where Jews were forced to live. Rebuilt between 1785 and 1787 by François Franque, the synagogue burned in 1845 and was rebuilt in 1846 by Joseph-Auguste Joffroy.
summaries.Q3584529: The Great Carmelites settled on the place des Carmes as early as 1267, outside the wall of the Commune. A rebuilding begun by John XXII in 1320 was still going on under Clement VI. The church was consecrated in 1520. A collapse in 1672 left only the front, the choir and the side chapels standing; the rebuilt church was blessed in 1678.
summaries.Q16855013: Of the convent of the Dames du Verbe Incarné, set up on the rue des Lices in 1639 by Jeanne Chézard de Matel, only this chapel remains, at no. 21, rebuilt by Jean-Baptiste Franque and his son François between 1725 and 1728 after a fire. Privately owned, it hosts each July the TOMA, Théâtres d'Outre-Mer en Avignon.
summaries.Q3527744: André Benedetto, his wife Jacqueline and Bertrand Hurault founded this theatre in 1963, at 6 place des Carmes, in the former Saint-Benoît parish hall belonging to the church of Saint-Symphorien-les-Carmes. Outside the theatre season, the place first served as a dance hall, a nightclub or a bowling alley.
summaries.Q1516274: The fabric of the present walls dates from the 14th and 15th centuries and runs for 4,330 metres. The moat that surrounded them was filled in when their surroundings were laid out: only the upper part of the walls is still visible. The marks cut by the stonemasons can still be made out in places.
summaries.Q6943577: The city's natural history museum was founded in 1840 by Esprit Requien, a botanist and palaeontologist from Avignon, as a natural history cabinet. Housed since 1940 in the hôtel de Raphélis-Soissan, over three floors, it traces the fauna and flora of the Vaucluse since prehistory.
summaries.Q22916640: On rue de la Bonneterie, the house first known as Puget de Chastueil owes its monumental staircase to a commission of 1695 from the marquis de Chastueil, to designs by Péru. Above the central first-floor window, the Puget arms are framed by two dogs whose carving was never finished. The ground floor holds shops.
summaries.Q22916652: The masons engaged to build this house for Jean-Pierre de Madon de Châteaublanc, to designs by Pierre II Mignard, signed their contract in 1687. The courtyard has a calade by Henri Barrelet strewn with comets, probably recalling the passage of Halley's comet in 1759. The panelling and painted overdoors are Louis XV.
summaries.Q2984016: This Gothic church faces the place Saint-Pierre. Its front, framed by two turrets, was finished in 1524; the solid walnut doors were carved by Antoine Volard in 1551 and are separated by a Virgin and Child attributed to Jean Péru. Made a collegiate church by Pope Innocent VI, it received the title of minor basilica in 2012.
summaries.Q38155000: The Discalced Carmelites settled in 1612 thanks to a gift from Claire de Pérussis, baroness of Oppède. Their convent was destroyed at their dispersal in 1792; some of the nuns regrouped in the rue du collège d'Annecy in 1801. The carmel was re-established in 1819 in the former Recollect convent, 3 rue de l'Observance, facing a one-hectare park.
summaries.Q22916611: Set up in the late 15th century by the town council to help the needy, the almshouse moved into this building in 1610. Its central block, of four storeys with an arcaded front, stands before the U-shaped wings. Bought by the city in 1845, the premises housed passing troops; the fine arts school held the east wing from 1890 to 1998.
summaries.Q36698400: Founded in 1975 by the principal dancers Catherine and Georges Golovine, the theatre occupies the former house of Canon Sylvain, in the Sainte-Catherine quarter, behind the Palais des Papes. Devoted to dance, it carries the "Off Danse" programme during the Festival Off. Yourik Golovine has run it since 2005.
summaries.Q16964583: Only one arch is still visible, the others being embedded in the walls of houses. 4.60 m high and 2.50 m wide, in large masonry, they form a retaining structure more than 250 m long bounding a wide esplanade that archaeological research identifies as the forum. The use of the space it framed remains uncertain.
summaries.Q15952870: An annexe of the musée Calvet, it brings together the city's archaeological collections in the former church of the Jesuit college, designed in 1616 by Étienne Martellange then handed over from 1620 to François de Royers de La Valfenière. Greek, Etruscan, Roman and early Christian antiquities and Gaulish art are shown.
summaries.Q22916642: Facing the hôtel de Crillon, built ten years later, it owes its street front to designs by François de Royers de La Valfenière. Paul de Fortia lodged Nicolas Mignard here, who painted in a gallery 18 panels from the Loves of Theagenes and Chariclea, sold in Paris in the 18th century. Seized at the Revolution, it was split into nos. 8 and 10.
summaries.Q22916654: Also called hôtel de Saint-Priest d'Urgel, the present building was probably put up after 1760 by the architect Jean-Baptiste II Péru, and has changed little since the survey of 1769. Inside it keeps a fine staircase and decorated rooms; Jean Pillement decorated the first-floor dining room, Jean Succharelli the boudoir.
summaries.Q334212: On avenue du Moulin-Notre-Dame, only the apse, the bell tower, the transept and the start of the nave survive of the abbey church. Seat of the canons regular of Saint-Ruf, the abbey became in the 12th century a chief centre of canonical reform, before the order's seat moved to Valence in 1158. The transept keeps battlements and arrow slits.
summaries.Q17635838: On rue des Vieilles Études, this former training house for Jesuit novices keeps a chapel designed by Étienne Martellange, a Greek cross under a dome, consecrated in 1611. The courtyard is lined on three sides by a vaulted gallery wrongly called a cloister. The north wing, rehabilitated in 1987 by Jean Nouvel, houses a hotel.
summaries.Q22916612: On rue Saint-Charles, the chapel was built by François Franque between 1749 and 1757, with the adjoining cloister and the street front, for the collège Saint-Charles-de-la-Croix, later a seminary. The choir, under a cloister vault, holds a huge baldachin by the Mazetti brothers, marble workers and sculptors in Avignon.
summaries.Q17640034: Created in 1983 by the director Alain Timár, a permanent stage and a Festival Off venue, it occupies a former Poor Clare convent founded in 1239, near the place Pie and the covered market from which it takes its name. A century after the foundation, it was in the convent chapel that Petrarch met Laure de Noves.
summaries.Q2873438: The Latin name of the city in antiquity. The town was born on the Rocher des Doms, occupied from the Neolithic and a control point on the Rhône, before spreading towards the alluvial plain. Made a Roman colony in the 2nd century under Hadrian, it gained walls, a forum and an aqueduct. From the 3rd century the urban area drew back to the rock.
summaries.Q24649065: A collection of 17th- and 18th-century decorative arts: Paris furniture, Moustiers and Marseille faience, silverware, Aubusson and Gobelins tapestries. It is shown in the Villeneuve-Esclapon mansion, bought in 1927 by the industrialist Louis Vouland, who left house and collections so a museum could open there.
summaries.Q22916658: Four secretaries of state were lodged here during Louis XIV's stay in Avignon in 1660. The building is attributed to the Royers de La Valfenière, father and son; the contract for the hall and staircase, signed in 1668, postdates the father's death. Handed to the Compagnons for a craft school, it is now divided into flats.
summaries.Q22916662: Simon Peilhon, a taffeta merchant, joined several houses on the rue du Puits-de-la-Rappe into a single residence from 1687, which his son rebuilt in 1711. Sold in Year II, the house became in 1838 the business premises of an iron merchant. Two carved figures inspired by those of Pierre Puget survive inside.
summaries.Q2983936: Former southern Gothic collegiate church at Villeneuve-lès-Avignon, in the Gard. A deed of 7 August 1333 raised the palace chapel of Cardinal Arnaud de Via, nephew of John XXII, into a collegiate church of twelve canons, endowed with that palace. The cloister dates from 1336, the belfry from 1362. The cardinal's effigy lies in the chapel of Relics.
summaries.Q1151040: A deconsecrated conventual church on the place des Corps-Saints, built near the tomb of Pierre de Luxembourg: the last foundation of the Avignon papacy and the city's only royal foundation. The works, halted in 1425, delivered only three bays of a plan for seven naves. The cloister opened to Festival performances in 1968.
summaries.Q22916614: At 13 rue Velouterie, the chapel was founded by Pope John XXII after a miracle in March 1320 during an execution at the stake. The pope paid for the choir, finished in 1327; the nave was completed only around 1340-1350. Secularised at the Revolution, it held a pump factory from 1932 to 1999, before private buyers took it over.
summaries.Q3452055: Lined by the Sorgue, the street once had twenty-three paddle wheels driving mills and silk works; the dyers who gave it its name used its water. Four wheels remain and people in Avignon call it rue des Roues. Paved with calades, it keeps the Cordeliers bell tower, the only remnant of the church where Laure was buried.
summaries.Q143463: Built on the Rocher des Doms, north of the city, the palace was in the 14th century the seat of Western Christendom and remains the largest Gothic building of the Middle Ages. It interlocks two structures: the old palace of Benedict XII, a fortress, and the new palace of Clement VI, whose frescoes Matteo Giovanetti directed.
summaries.Q3078019: On Mont Andaon, above Villeneuve-lès-Avignon, this fortified wall 750 metres long was built during the second half of the 14th century, facing the lands of the Empire and the popes. Jean de Loubières, architect of the Palais des Papes, completed it on the orders of Charles V. From the twin towers the view reaches Avignon.
summaries.Q22916663: On rue de la Bonneterie, the merchant Jean-Paul Raoulx bought two adjoining houses in 1692 and had Jean Péru put up in their place a residence on the scale of a private mansion. Above the door, a balcony bears a helmeted head of Minerva, and mascarons decorate the ground-floor windows.
summaries.Q281849: Laid out in the 19th century as an English garden on top of the rock, beside the Palais des Papes, this 3-hectare public garden gathers lawns, a lake, rockeries and a vineyard planted with the 12 main côtes-du-rhône grape varieties. Its terrace gives a viewpoint 30 m up over the Rhône and the Pont Saint-Bénézet.
summaries.Q2315439: Born of the will of Cardinal Bertrand de Deaux, the collegiate church was built in three years and four months and consecrated in 1359. It passes for the most characteristic building of Avignon Gothic. The first chapel on the right holds a Christ Carrying the Cross by Francesco Laurana, commissioned by King René in 1478.
summaries.Q2957347: Baroque chapel of the Visitandine convent, its front opens onto the place de la Pignotte. Cardinal Mario Filonardi, vice-legate of Avignon and patron of the convent, laid its first stone on 10 April 1631; it was consecrated in 1638. A church "in the Roman manner", it is among the very first examples on this side of the Alps.
summaries.Q22916613: At the corner of the rue du Général-Leclerc and the rue Saint-Jean-le-Vieux, this chapel was built in 1770 by Jean-Baptiste Lambertin for the Sainte-Garde seminary, and consecrated in 1775. After the Revolution it served as a courtroom and a commodity exchange. It is now part of the conservatoire Olivier Messiaen.
summaries.Q2174601: From the place du Portail Matheron to the porte Saint-Lazare, this street was the main way into the city from the Comtat Venaissin and the only one leading straight from a gate in the walls to the Palais des Papes. At no. 20, the Augustinian bell tower, built between 1372 and 1377, has leaned slightly since the 1907 earthquake.
summaries.Q1664416: Housed in the former residence of the archbishops of Avignon, a 14th-century building next to the Palais des Papes, the museum opened in 1976. Its collections, spread over nineteen rooms, bring together 326 Italian primitives by more than 130 artists, mostly from the Campana collection, and works of the Avignon school.
summaries.Q2961249: Founded at Villeneuve-lès-Avignon by a bull of Pope Innocent VI of 2 June 1356, the charterhouse adjoined the palace that pope had built for himself; its church and cloister were consecrated on 19 August 1358. Sold in seventeen lots in 1794, then bought back plot by plot by the State, it has been a cultural meeting centre since 1973.
summaries.Q22916626: On the place des Trois-Pilats, the house bought in 1706 by Joseph Gasqui was rebuilt in the second quarter of the 18th century: a document of 1744 calls it just rebuilt. It was the seat of the Illuminés d'Avignon, a sect founded by Dom Pernety, who died there in 1796. Listed in 1932, it has held 14 flats since February 2022.
summaries.Q292378: A river island in the Rhône, the largest on the river, formed by the gradual joining of a string of islets including the île Piot, which forms its southern tip. Ceded by Villeneuve-lès-Avignon in 1856, it is a district of Avignon still farmed, made of mas, houses and campsites. A free river shuttle serves the Avignon bank.
summaries.Q2983940: Tradition credits Saint Agricol, bishop of Avignon around 660 to 700, with building a church on this site; excavations have uncovered early Christian burials there. Raised from its ruins in the 10th century, it was made a collegiate church by John XXII in 1321. The front, forecourt and monumental stair date from the 15th century.
summaries.Q2957417: On rue de la Banasterie, the chapel was that of the Black Penitents of Mercy, a brotherhood founded in 1586 by Pompée Catilina to help prisoners and attend the condemned. Its front, rebuilt from 1739, shows a glory carved in the round: a cloud of angels bearing the head of Saint John the Baptist on a dish.
summaries.Q19404022: On the place Crillon, this late 16th-century building took its classical look during the major works carried out in 1740 by François de Boutin de Valouse, then became the hôtel de Graveson in 1775. Catherine Pierron bought it on 25 September 1799 and the same year made it the Hôtel d'Europe. It has 39 rooms and 5 suites.
summaries.Q284444: Completed in 1185, the bridge crossed the Rhône; floods and wars cut it back over the centuries and only four arches remain, clinging to the left bank. It sets out from north Avignon towards the Gard but no longer gets there. On one of the piers stands the chapelle Saint-Bénézet, topped by the chapelle Saint-Nicolas.
